You can hear it in Richard Strauss's Salome, Elektra and An Alpine Symphony, and in Varèse's Amériques and Arcana. In chamber music, Hindemith's Trio for heckelphone, viola and piano and Gordon Jacob's Variations on Annie Laurie show its use in a small ensemble. There are also Kalevi Aho's operas, symphonies and concertos, an oboe quartet in William P. Perry's film score, and wind-band works by Cecil Burleigh.
海克爾管主要採用高級木材製造，通常使用烏木或楓木製作管身，這些木材提供良好的音響: The heckelphone is made mainly of good wood, usually ebony or maple for the body, and these woods give good acoustic properties and durability. The double reed is made of cane, which produces its distinctive vibrating tone colour. Cork may be used inside the instrument to make the joints airtight. The metal fittings include keywork of brass or another alloy, precisely made to keep the tuning and the mechanism reliable. A leather sleeve may protect the outside.
海克爾管屬氣鳴雙簧樂器，演奏時以吹管連接雙簧片與管身，簧片近似巴松管或大型英國管: The heckelphone is a double-reed aerophone. In playing, a bocal connects the double reed to the body, and the reed is close to a bassoon reed or a large cor anglais reed. The instrument is about 1.3 metres long and stands on the floor on a short metal peg below the bell. The fingering is the same as the oboe and cor anglais, with the keys laid out after the bassoon; the music is read in treble clef and sounds an octave lower. For chamber music a muted bell can be fitted. A beginner must first get used to joining reed and bocal, to the peg support, to oboe fingering and to reading treble clef an octave down.

Its range lies an octave below the oboe and reaches down to A, roughly A2 to G5; the music is written in treble clef and sounds an octave lower. A muted bell can be fitted to reduce the volume for small ensembles. Compared with the instruments of its family it sits between the oboe, the cor anglais and the bassoon, mainly filling the bass of the oboe group.

The heckelphone is a double-reed aerophone from Germany, of the oboe family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.112-71. It was developed by Wilhelm Heckel and his son and launched in 1904; the outline is close to the oboe but the bore is wider and the range an octave lower, down to A. The player connects the double reed with a bocal, the fingering is the same as the oboe, and the music is written in treble clef though it sounds an octave lower; the body is about 1.3 metres long, needs a metal peg to stand on, and a muted bell can be fitted. Richard Strauss's Salome and other works used it first, and it also appears in Varèse's orchestral music and Hindemith's chamber music; it is commonly used in large orchestras to fill the gap between oboe and bassoon.
海克爾管起源於德國，由威廉·海克爾及其子研發；其構想可追溯至1879年理察·瓦格: The heckelphone originated in Germany, developed by Wilhelm Heckel and his son; the idea can be traced to a suggestion by Richard Wagner in 1879, and the instrument appeared in 1904. It is a double-reed instrument, an octave below the oboe, meant to fill the gap between oboe and bassoon in a large orchestra. Richard Strauss used it early in Salome and other works, and it later appeared in orchestral and chamber music by Varèse, Chávez, Copland and Hindemith. It is still rare, with about 150 made, and an extended model, the Lupophon, can play lower still.
